prize_parts.citation: for developing methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets with endogenous prices, and models of dynamic industries, which made structural empirical industrial organisation a quantitative basis for analysing market power, mergers and welfare

statement.case_for: My preferred part is still B001, but I have changed the third laureate from Bresnahan to Levinsohn. The round-1 exchange changed my view of the unit of the prize, not of the merit of the field. My own citation was a programme-level one, running from demand-based measurement of market power through production-function methods to dynamic industries. Seven colleagues, and the chair's questions, pushed me to ask which citation the Committee can defend precisely. The answer is a method-level one: random-coefficients demand with endogenous prices and equilibrium supply, plus the Ericson-Pakes dynamic-industry framework. For that citation the identifiable originators are Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. The 1995 paper is jointly authored, and leaving out one author while keeping the other two splits the credit for a single result. The Committee would have to explain that split, and I found no good way to explain it. The case on merit is unchanged. The tools are original, changed what can be measured (substitution, markups, merger counterfactuals, welfare), have been used for about three decades in academic work and regulation, and have spread to trade, health, environmental and productivity work. On the chair's toolkit-versus-discovery question, my criterion is this. A method counts as a discovery-enabling advance if it makes a previously unanswerable question answerable, if it changes practice outside its home field, and if the main objections have been studied and are understood. I judge B001 to meet all three on the evidence colleagues cite, though that evidence comes from background knowledge.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is that I now back a citation that leaves out Bresnahan, who set the agenda that BLP made operational. A method-level prize can read as rewarding the tool and not the programme behind it, and the three-name cap makes that cost unavoidable. Reiss, Benkard and Levin are also left out. Pakes's production-function and dynamic-game work is only partly covered by this citation. A Committee that sees a toolkit as a lesser kind of contribution than a substantive finding could reasonably rank B001 below B002 or B013. The applied results are also sensitive to functional form, numerical implementation, instruments and weak identification. I think these sensitivities are well documented and mostly understood, but I have not verified that independently.

responses.point: Hassler (chair) keeps Levinsohn because the citation is about a method defined by one named paper, and he warns that widening it to production-function estimation or the new empirical IO programme would blur the unit of the prize and reopen attribution. He also keeps Kiyotaki and Moore as the clean B002 pair.
responses.response: This moved me. My round-1 citation was the wide one, and I now see that it invited the attribution problem I was trying to solve with Bresnahan. A narrow method-level unit is easier to defend. It is also easier to defend if someone asks why Pakes, but not every strand of his work, is credited. I accept that naming Bresnahan over Levinsohn makes sense only under a different programme-level prize, and I am not proposing that one. I also agree with him on B002. If the Committee turns to it, Kiyotaki and Moore are the pair, and I would not add Gertler.

responses.point: Andersson holds Levinsohn in the third slot and says leaving him out while keeping Berry would split the authorship of the one paper that defines the method. He would accept Bresnahan only under an agenda-based citation, reworded so it does not credit the BLP paper itself.
responses.response: I now agree with the structure of this argument. My earlier position gave a programme-level reason but kept a citation that read as method-level, and that mismatch is the weakness he identifies. I resolve it by changing the name. I keep the method-level citation, and Levinsohn takes the third slot. I do not accept that Bresnahan's contribution is merely programmatic, since I still think it is foundational. But foundational credit and credit for the specific estimator are separate questions. I also note that he keeps B050 as his first alternative, and I list it second after B002 for similar reasons.

responses.point: Friberg argues that the citation should follow the discovery being rewarded. He would keep it to demand estimation and market power, with dynamic oligopoly and production functions as supporting context, so that Pakes's strands do not all have to be apportioned among many co-authors.
responses.response: I agree, and I adopt that framing in the citation. It still names dynamic-industry models, since Pakes's Ericson-Pakes framework is the part that takes the measurement toward entry, exit and investment. I would leave production-function estimation out of the text, as he suggests. His point that the contribution is a measurement discovery, not just a technique, is also the best answer to the chair's question about toolkits. I do think the Bresnahan omission is a real cost and not a matter of merit equivalence. I accept it as a cost of the three-name cap.

responses.point: Boppart prefers B050 with Melitz and Helpman, and wants the citation tied tightly to firm heterogeneity and selection so that Helpman's political-economy work (B021) stays out. He concedes that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and Redding, are real attribution costs.
responses.response: I agree that Helpman's credit belongs in the firm-heterogeneity achievement and that B021 should not enter the citation. My question is about attribution, which he himself calls the real risk. A two-name Melitz-Helpman design leaves out Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum, who sit outside this ballot entry, and Redding, who is inside it. The Committee would have to explain both omissions, and I do not think that can be done cleanly. That is why B050 is my second alternative and not my preferred part, and I do not think it is a weaker idea. A Melitz-only version would be cleaner on the surface, but I find it hard to justify given Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple. I note my co-authorship with him in the conflict note.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson prefers B013 and defends the three-name set with Katz. She names B001 as the strongest alternative and accepts that B001 has the longer record of durability and adoption, while calling it mostly a toolkit prize.
responses.response: I accept her toolkit point as the central open question. My criterion is above, and I think B001 meets it. On B013, I still see a framework-and-evidence split that B001 does not have. The task and skill-premium strand and the China-shock strand have different cores, and the magnitudes of the shock effects remain contested. A single-strand version would help, but then the three-name question returns, with Katz versus Dorn, and I do not see a principled way to settle it. I would not call her preference unreasonable. My concern is that the credit boundary is less settled than B001's. On the combined entry, my own two-name Autor-Katz version looks too narrow now.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee prefers a method-level citation (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn) or a programme-level one in which Bresnahan would belong. I now lean to the former, but the choice is a judgement and I have no independent evidence to settle it.

How the Committee weighs a measurement toolkit against a substantive discovery. My criterion is that a method must make a previously unanswerable question answerable, change practice beyond its home field and have its main sensitivities understood.

How far applied BLP-type results change in practice with numerical implementation, instrument choice and functional form. I have not verified citation, adoption or regulatory-use claims independently.
Whether a single achievement is best. I think adding a second achievement within three names would weaken the citation, since B001 already uses all three places.

If the Committee turned to B002, whether the Kiyotaki-Moore pair leaves enough distinct ground relative to Bernanke's 2022 prize. I think the collateral-constraint mechanism is distinct from the bank-run and crisis analysis, but the empirical identification of the channel is more model-dependent than for B001.
statement.conflict_note: Updated from round 1. I am the secretary. I have no listed co-authorship or institutional tie to Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn or Bresnahan, or to Kiyotaki or Moore. I do have ties to colleagues who argue for other configurations. Timo Boppart (co-opted member) is a frequent co-author, including on the 2018 Myrdal Prize article, and prefers B050, which is my second alternative. John Hassler (chair) is a long-term co-author and an IIES colleague. Both are committee colleagues and not candidates. Neither tie involves a credited name on B001, B002 or B050. My work on technology and inequality (capital-skill complementarity) and on heterogeneous agents is topically adjacent to B013 and B039, which I do not propose. These ties are disclosed and not adjudicated.
